scope: Source-backed reconstruction of the public Orion navigation and state-estimation architecture, onboard sensor measurement roles, Deep Space Network ground-navigation context, Artemis Real-time Orbit Website public state-vector products, and selected Artemis II as-flown navigation evidence while explicitly separating public architecture and mission products from unavailable onboard navigation-filter states, raw sensor histories, ground orbit-determination solution histories, estimator residuals, innovations, covariance, gains, bias states, measurement-selection histories, and measurement accept-reject histories.

sources.title: Avionics and Software
claims_used: Orion GNC&P flight software runs on the vehicle management computers and receives inputs from navigation sensors.
Orion has an onboard navigation system composed of redundant sensors used for position and attitude knowledge.
Orion inertial measurement units supply inertial data used by the vehicle management computers to compute position, velocity, and attitude.
GPS receivers provide position and velocity updates during ascent, low-Earth orbit, and reentry.
Barometric altimeters provide atmospheric-pressure-derived altitude and backup entry deployment altitude information.
Star trackers determine spacecraft attitude during orbital operations.
The optical navigation camera uses Earth and Moon imagery to determine range and bearing and supports emergency-return capability.
Sun sensors determine Sun direction during emergency safe mode.
Outside GPS range in deep space, Deep Space Network measurements support determination of Orion's location.

sources.title: Track NASA's Artemis II Mission in Real Time
claims_used: AROW provides public tracking information for Orion.
NASA describes state vectors as data describing where Orion is located and how it moves.
AROW provides state vectors to the public.
NASA provides downloadable Artemis II trajectory data described as an ephemeris.
AROW visualizes mission data associated with Orion and Mission Control.

sources.title: Artemis 2 Optical Navigation (OpNav) camera
claims_used: The Artemis II optical navigation camera is a Pixelink Prometheus PL-D725.
The camera is hard-mounted on the starboard lower side of the Crew Module Adapter.
Its primary use is spacecraft navigation during flight.
The camera captured images of Earth during Artemis II.
The camera captured images of the Moon during Artemis II.

sources.title: Artemis II Mission Milestones: An Image and Video Recap
claims_used: NASA publicly identifies a Flight Day 1 black-and-white Earth image as having been captured by the optical navigation sensor on Orion.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Update: Proximity Operations Complete, Perigee Raise Burn Up Next
claims_used: The Artemis II crew successfully completed the proximity-operations demonstration.
The demonstration used Orion's onboard navigation sensors.
The demonstration used reaction-control thrusters.
The public report does not identify a complete sensor-by-sensor measurement history or relative-state time history.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 5: Crew Demos Suits, Readies for Lunar Flyby
claims_used: Ahead of the outbound correction burn, NASA reported that Jeremy Hansen would monitor spacecraft configuration and navigation data.
This pre-burn report is not promoted to a complete as-flown navigation-display history.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 7: First Return Correction Burn Complete
claims_used: During the completed first return correction burn, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen reviewed procedures and monitored spacecraft configuration and navigation data.
The public report does not identify the exact displayed navigation variables.

This planning statement is not promoted to an as-flown navigation-display history.

claims_used: During the completed third return correction burn, the Artemis II crew reviewed procedures and monitored spacecraft configuration and navigation data.
The public report does not identify the exact displayed navigation variables.

products.role: Onboard spacecraft position, velocity, and attitude knowledge computed from navigation inputs.
Ground-based determination of spacecraft location or trajectory using measurements such as Deep Space Network communication-signal observations.
Public downloadable state-vector and trajectory information describing Orion's location and motion.

guardrails: Public navigation-sensor architecture is not an as-flown sensor time history.
IMU capability is not a raw Artemis II inertial-measurement history.
A star-tracker role is not a published Artemis II attitude-solution history.
GPS capability is not a complete as-flown Artemis II GPS solution history.
Deep Space Network tracking is external ground navigation support and is not an onboard navigation sensor.
Deep Space Network ground navigation is not the Orion onboard navigation filter.
GROUND_ORBIT_DETERMINATION is a MissionLab normalized taxonomy category and is not claimed to be the exact public name of a NASA Artemis II data product.
An Artemis II optical-navigation image is as-flown sensor evidence but is not an estimator residual or innovation history.
Optical-navigation image capture does not prove a specific estimator measurement update.
AROW public state vectors are not proven to be the Orion onboard navigation-filter state.
An AROW public state vector is not proven to be the complete ground orbit-determination solution.
A public OEM is a trajectory data product and is not raw spacecraft telemetry.
A public OEM solution-to-solution difference is not a navigation error.
A public OEM solution-to-solution difference is not measured maneuver delta-v.
An OEM product creation time does not by itself prove measurement assimilation or maneuver assimilation.
Crew monitoring of navigation data does not expose the complete onboard navigation-state history.
Crew monitoring of navigation data does not establish that displayed values are identical to the complete onboard filter state.
As-flown crew navigation-data monitoring is explicitly confirmed here for RTC1 and RTC3 and is not generalized to every trajectory-correction burn without equivalent public evidence.
Pre-burn or planned monitoring language is not silently promoted to an as-flown display history.
The absence of a navigation record from the current curated public source set is not proof that the record never existed.
